In Trinidadian guppy (HP Marianne96) (Poecilia reticulata HP Mrn96), individuals reared under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] reach a maximum standard length of 3.73 cm [Li = 3.73 cm], a value that represents the upper limit of somatic growth observed in this particular high-predation population. This measurement was obtained from a long-term captive breeding study in which males and females were measured repeatedly throughout their lifetimes, and the asymptote of the growth curve was estimated using non-linear mixed-effects models. The relatively modest body size compared to some other guppy populations from low-predation environments is consistent with the classic life-history trade-off between rapid maturation and reduced asymptotic size, which is thought to be mediated by the selective pressure of elevated predation risk in the Marianne stream. Field surveys conducted in the same habitat have corroborated this laboratory finding, with the largest individuals collected rarely exceeding 3.5 cm, suggesting that the laboratory estimate of maximum standard length is biologically realistic. The consistent thermal regime of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] used in these experiments matches the average water temperature recorded in the source stream during the dry season, further supporting the ecological relevance of these measurements. This species has been the subject of extensive comparative work on the evolution of life-history strategies across the Poeciliidae, and the values reported here align well with predictions from theory regarding the effects of size-selective predation on body size at maturity.

Under the same thermal conditions of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the mean age at birth in this population varies with food availability. Under high food conditions, the mean age at birth is approximately 24.4 days [ab = approximately 24.4 days], while under low food conditions, it is about 24.9 days [ab = about 24.9 days] at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This slight delay under reduced resource levels is consistent with the expected deceleration of embryonic development when maternal provisioning is limited, a pattern documented in other Poecilia reticulata populations. These values were recorded in a controlled laboratory experiment where females were housed individually and monitored daily for parturition. The yolk-sac larvae emerge fully developed and commence exogenous feeding shortly after birth. The observed ages at birth align with the known range for the species under similar thermal regimes, although populations from different streams can exhibit considerable variation depending on local selective pressures. These data contribute to a broader understanding of how resource availability influences early life-history traits in live-bearing fishes.
